content: The recommendations for contraceptive use in the revised Selected Practice Recommendations (SPR) are categorized as either strong or conditional. A strong recommendation indicates that the Guideline Development Group (GDG) is confident that the benefits of the recommendation outweigh the risks, making it suitable for adoption as policy in most situations. On the other hand, conditional recommendations are issued when there is uncertainty about the balance of benefits and harms. These require further discussion and input from various stakeholders before being implemented as policy, as outlined in the second edition of the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. Despite the generally low or very low quality of evidence, most updated recommendations in the third edition of the SPR were classified as strong. The recommendations are presented in a narrative format to maintain consistency with previous editions. For recommendations regarding examinations and tests before initiating contraceptive methods, an A-B-C classification system is used to determine the necessity of specific procedures for the safe provision of the method. The GDG reached consensus on new and revised recommendations while maintaining the majority of existing ones. This consensus was achieved through discussions, debates, and expert consultations, with unanimous agreement among GDG members. A draft of the SPR document was reviewed by an external peer review group of six experts who were not part of the GDG meeting. Their feedback was addressed and incorporated into the final guidance, which was approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee on May 25, 2016. The third edition of the SPR includes new recommendations, such as the addition of Sino-implant (II) as a contraceptive method. This implant, containing levonorgestrel (LNG), is a two-rod system approved for four years of use. The GDG determined that the recommendations for initiating Sino-implant (II) are the same as those for other progestogen-only implants. A woman can start using Sino-implant (II) within seven days of the start of her menstrual bleeding or at any other time if it is reasonably certain she is not pregnant. Recommendations for additional protection and specific scenarios, such as postpartum or post-abortion use, are also provided. The strength of this recommendation is classified as strong, despite the lack of direct evidence, based on indirect evidence from studies on other progestogen-only implants. Regarding examinations and tests before initiating Sino-implant (II), the GDG concluded that the requirements are the same as for other contraceptive implants. The strength of this recommendation is also classified as strong. The duration of use for Sino-implant (II) aligns with the product labeling, which states it can be used for up to four years. Evidence suggests the implant remains highly effective for at least four years, with some studies indicating effectiveness through the fifth year. However, evidence beyond five years is limited. The GDG classified this recommendation as strong, emphasizing the importance of preventing unintended pregnancies while considering the available evidence. No routine follow-up is required after initiating Sino-implant (II), consistent with recommendations for other contraceptive implants. Follow-up visits should address any issues, such as side effects or method use, and provide counseling on protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The GDG determined that unnecessary follow-up requirements could pose barriers to continued contraceptive use. This recommendation is also classified as strong. The GDG emphasized the importance of considering women's values and preferences, including factors such as choice, ease of use, side effects, and efficacy, in developing these recommendations. The goal is to facilitate access to contraceptive methods while maintaining safety and effectiveness based on the available evidence.
